events.title: Telegram
events.text:
🇩🇪🇫🇷🇬🇧‼️ According to General Fabien Mandon, Chief of Staff of the French Armed Forces, Germany has decided to withdraw from the Franco-German program for the development of the next-generation main battle tank (MGCS). This decision represents another significant blow to defense cooperation between the two countries, especially after the joint Franco-German-Spanish program for the development of a sixth-generation fighter (FCAS) was also canceled four months ago.
♦️ The MGCS project began in 2017 and aimed to replace tanks of the French Leclerc and German Leopard 2 types with a new generation of combat systems by approximately 2040-2045. However, the program has been hampered for years by disagreements over funding, technology development, and the division of work between French and German companies.
♦️ According to General Mandon, Germany's withdrawal is a significant loss in industrial terms, but years of joint work have helped to shape the basic concept of the next-generation tank. He also noted that France still needs heavy armored vehicles and the development of new combat systems, including the use of artificial intelligence and unmanned technologies.
♦️ At the same time, against the backdrop of problems in military cooperation between France and Germany, the United Kingdom is offering Berlin the opportunity for a new partnership in the defense sector. British Prime Minister Rishi Sunak announced after a meeting with German Chancellor Olaf Scholz in Berlin that London is ready to invite Germany to join the international program for the development of a sixth-generation fighter (GCAP), which the United Kingdom is implementing with Italy and Japan.
🗣️ "I told the Chancellor that the United Kingdom is open to Germany joining the GCAP program. This issue should be developed with our partners, Italy and Japan, in the coming period," Sunak said.
♦️ The development of a new generation of combat aircraft within the GCAP framework is planned for 2035. The program involves British BAE Systems, Italian Leonardo, and Japanese Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. The future fighter will be equipped with advanced sensors and artificial intelligence systems, and is designed to operate in conjunction with unmanned combat platforms.
♦️ Germany's possible participation could help to expand the program's funding and technological capabilities. However, the addition of a new partner will require agreement among the participating countries. The position of Japan is particularly important, as Tokyo is interested in ensuring that the development of the new fighter does not slow down and that the project is completed on schedule.
♦️ At this stage, Germany has not yet made a decision about joining GCAP. Nevertheless, following the collapse of two major joint military programs with France, the rapprochement between Berlin and London could lead to significant changes in the European defense industry and the direction of development of next-generation military technologies.

The Navy’s real readiness assessment after the USS Abraham Lincoln’s marathon deployment and other war commitments is “artificially high,” Vice Chief of Naval Operations Adm. James Kilby has warned. 
He called the picture “a false positive,” addressing the National Commission on the Future of the Navy.
The true cost will surface later, he added.
Key pressures:
🌏 ships remain deployed or haven’t returned for maintenance, artificially inflating readiness rates
🌏 deferred maintenance and skipped modernization to meet short-term combat demands
🌏 shipyards face looming backlog as vessels return
🌏 compressed training cycles leave crews with little flexibility
🌏 unmanned systems could ease demand for full carrier or amphibious groups, but that option is still years away
The sober assessment came a day after War Secretary Pete Hegseth praised sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln for a record deployment of 265 consecutive days without a port call during the US war on Iran.

🇮🇱 Israel’s Elbit expands arms footprint in Morocco, eyes NATO buyers
Seeking to establish itself as a regional arms production and export hub, Morocco is moving deeper to embed Israeli technology into its defense manufacturing, reports Reuters.
Moroccan Military Industry (MMI), a subsidiary of [Israeli defense giant Elbit System](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70635)s, will begin delivering armored vehicle turrets to the Moroccan army in March 2027.
MMI’s expansion spans several areas:
➡️ production: existing weapons systems plant near Casablanca and a second facility under development in Sidi Yahya for medium- and large-caliber ammunition
➡️ anti-drone weapons: turret variant using radar-triggered ammunition that sprays tungsten fragments to destroy drones, offering a lower-cost defense against cheap aerial threats
➡️ new systems & exports: plans for vehicle-mounted self-propelled mortars, with Morocco serving as an export hub
MMI expects to supply an unnamed European NATO country, according to General Manager Kaduri Naor.
The expansion comes after Morocco normalized relations with Israel in 2020, with ties further flourishing after [the Ceuta migrant crisis,](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73188) which[ Chinese intel branded ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73188)a textbook hybrid operation enabled by Israel.
The relationship upgrade has faced strong [domestic opposition.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75204)

events.text:
📹 Palantir & other US defense contractors warn of rare earth crunch and soaring prices
The US military-industrial complex is warning that Project Vault, a plan to stockpile critical minerals, could drive prices even higher, the Financial Times reports.
Project Vault is a $12 billion brainchild of the US Export-Import Bank aimed at building a strategic domestic reserve of scarce rare earth metals that civilian industries could tap during shortages.
The Aerospace Industries Association (AIA), a US trade group representing military and aerospace firms including Palantir and BAE Systems, warns that Project Vault could end up “competing” for critical minerals “amid an already constrained global supply."
The US is facing a rare earth shortage as China tightens export controls amid a simmering Sino-American trade spat. In 2025, 71% of US rare-earth imports critical to defense and energy came from China. That leaves the US military and civilian industries competing for the same critical minerals.
The pressure is set to grow. From January 1, US defense contractors will be barred from sourcing rare earths, permanent magnets, and critical minerals from China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea for military use.
In March, US defense industry sources told S&P Global that shortages of tungsten, antimony, gallium, and germanium already represent a strategic vulnerability for the US military in the event of a prolonged war with Iran.
🔴If the US is running out of tungsten and antimony and it doesn't have access to germanium and gallium supplies, it cannot build new weapons,🔴 warned Peter Clausi, director of the Critical Minerals Institute, a Toronto-based think tank.
